case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a plaintiff can pursue a Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution claim under § 1983 for a baseless charge that contributed to a prosecutorial seizure when another simultaneously filed charge was supported by probable cause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. IV (Fourth Amendment—unreasonable seizures, including seizures pursuant to legal process) and 42 U.S.C. § 1983 (civil action for deprivation of rights).
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue that the Sixth Circuit’s “any-crime” rule is wrong because Fourth Amendment liability should turn on whether the specific charge challenged was supported by probable cause and whether that baseless charge caused or prolonged an unreasonable seizure (e.g., detention, bond conditions, travel limits, court appearances). Even if one charge had probable cause, officers should remain liable for initiating or maintaining additional unsupported charges that foreseeably increase the severity or duration of the seizure, undermine the Warrant/Probable Cause requirements, and create incentives to stack charges to shield misconduct. Petitioners and supporting amici emphasize that each charge can independently alter bail, pretrial restrictions, leverage in plea bargaining, and reputational and liberty harms, so probable cause for one offense should not categorically immunize fabrication or reckless charging on another.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents defend a rule under which there is no Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution liability (or no compensable Fourth Amendment injury) when the plaintiff’s seizure was already justified by at least one charge supported by probable cause. In their view, the Fourth Amendment is concerned with the reasonableness of the seizure as a whole; if lawful probable cause existed to seize and hold the person on any charge, then the plaintiff cannot establish the required lack of probable cause/causation element for a malicious-prosecution-type Fourth Amendment claim based on another charge. Supporting amici for respondents further contend that a plaintiff must at minimum show the unsupported charge changed the nature or duration of the seizure (e.g., increased detention time or restrictions), and warn that allowing claim-by-claim litigation would expand municipal and officer liability and complicate causation and damages.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Devenpeck point is the best for Respondent, but it concerns the objective justification for an initial arrest and does not answer Manuel’s distinct inquiry into continued restraint “pursuant to legal process,” where the legality of the process actually used depends on probable cause. Justice Thomas is right that causation must do real limiting work: if the baseless count did not prolong detention, increase bail, or materially worsen conditions, there is no Fourth Amendment injury attributable to that count. But adopting an “any-crime” categorical rule would sweep too broadly by insulating unsupported add-on charges that foreseeably ratchet up restraints, which is hard to reconcile with Thompson’s malicious-prosecution analogue and the Fourth Amendment’s focus on the reasonableness of the seizure as imposed. The narrow, institutionally modest path is a charge-specific lack-of-probable-cause inquiry coupled with a requirement of incremental restraint and ordinary causation/damages limits.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett most forcefully contend that Manuel and Thompson require a charge-specific Fourth Amendment inquiry, tempered by “incremental restraint” causation. But the Fourth Amendment’s text asks whether the seizure was “unreasonable,” and if lawful process supported by probable cause for one charge would have produced the same custody and conditions, the overall seizure is not rendered unreasonable merely because an additional count lacked probable cause—§ 1983 causation cannot be satisfied by a non-causal defect. Manuel confirms the Fourth Amendment governs post-process detention, yet it does not establish that every unsupported charge is independently actionable absent proof it actually prolonged detention or materially worsened restrictions; that is a damages question, not a stand-alone constitutional violation. Devenpeck, while in the arrest context, supports the broader originalist point that probable cause to seize is not inherently charge-bound, and I see no historical basis to constitutionalize a charge-by-charge overcharging tort.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Barrett’s “charge-specific but only with incremental restraint” proposal is the best narrowing move on the other side, but it still assumes—without clear Fourth Amendment textual or historical support—that each count is a freestanding constitutional unit even when the plaintiff would have been seized and held on a concededly valid, probable-cause-supported charge. Manuel and Thompson do require a seizure pursuant to legal process that is unlawful, yet neither decision compels a charge-by-charge constitutionalization where the challenged count did not alter the fact, duration, or severity of the restraint; on a practical view of reasonableness, that is the whole seizure. Devenpeck, though an arrest case, reinforces the basic Fourth Amendment point that probable cause is a justification for the seizure itself, not a guarantee of perfectly curated charging documents, and importing a charge-specific regime risks turning § 1983 into an overcharging tort with predictable chilling effects on ordinary enforcement. I agree with Justice Thomas that causation must do real work: absent proof the unsupported count itself caused materially greater detention or restrictions, there is no Fourth Amendment injury attributable to that count.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Devenpeck’s any-offense concept suggests probable cause is not charge-bound, but Devenpeck dealt with the objective validity of an initial warrantless arrest—not the distinct Manuel problem of continued restraint “pursuant to legal process” that is allegedly maintained through an unsupported charge. Justice Thomas is right to insist on causation: if the baseless count truly did not increase detention, bail, or conditions, § 1983 should not allow recovery for that count—but that limits liability through incremental-restraint causation rather than creating categorical immunity. I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Thompson’s malicious-prosecution analogue points toward a charge-specific probable-cause inquiry focused on the particular process that imposed or prolonged the seizure, while ordinary causation/damages rules prevent this from becoming a general overcharging tort. An any-crime rule would, in practice, insulate baseless add-on charges that predictably worsen outcomes for vulnerable defendants, which is hard to reconcile with the Fourth Amendment’s reasonableness and probable-cause requirements as applied to the legal process actually restraining liberty.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Devenpeck-based “any-crime” point is the best argument for Respondent, but Devenpeck resolves whether an arrest is objectively justified at inception—not whether a later seizure “pursuant to legal process” is reasonable when that very process is driven in part by a charge lacking probable cause. As the Chief Justice notes, Manuel and Thompson tie this Fourth Amendment claim to a malicious-prosecution analogue, which is naturally charge-specific and focused on the legal process that actually restrains liberty. I agree with Justice Thomas that causation must do real limiting work, but that supports a narrow rule (no liability absent proof the baseless charge caused incremental detention, bail, or conditions), not a categorical immunity whenever any other charge had probable cause. Treating the entire seizure as automatically reasonable because one count was supported collapses the probable-cause requirement for the legal process itself and invites foreseeable overcharging without meaningful Fourth Amendment scrutiny.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Devenpeck point is the strongest for Respondent, but Devenpeck addressed whether an arrest is justified at inception if probable cause exists for any offense; it did not create an across-the-board “any-crime” shield for later detention maintained pursuant to specified legal process. Manuel makes clear the Fourth Amendment continues to regulate post-process pretrial detention, and the constitutional question becomes whether the particular process that imposed or maintained restraints was supported by probable cause, not whether some other charge could have justified some seizure in the abstract. I agree with Justice Thomas that causation must be doing real work, but that is best implemented (as Chief Justice Roberts suggests) through a charge-specific, incremental-restraint requirement rather than an atextual categorical bar that would immunize unsupported add-on charges even when they foreseeably increase bail, detention, or conditions. On a textualist and separation-of-powers approach, we should not displace the Amendment’s probable-cause requirement with a judicially invented immunity when ordinary § 1983 causation and damages principles can do the limiting.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Alito’s best point is that Devenpeck’s any-offense principle cautions against making Fourth Amendment reasonableness turn on the label of the charge, and I share the concern about turning § 1983 into an overcharging tort. But Devenpeck was about a warrantless arrest’s objective justification at the inception of the seizure; it does not answer the Manuel/Thompson setting where continued restraint is imposed “pursuant to legal process,” and the specific counts can drive bail, detention duration, or conditions. Justice Thomas’s causation emphasis is correct as a limiting principle, yet it supports the Chief Justice Roberts/Justice Barrett formulation: no liability unless the unsupported count caused incremental restraint beyond what the supported count would have produced, which preserves Fourth Amendment doctrine and institutional administrability without a categorical any-crime bar. That narrow rule fits history and precedent while avoiding unnecessary expansion of damages liability.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Justice Alito’s strongest point is that Devenpeck’s “any-offense” principle suggests probable cause for one charge renders the seizure reasonable, but that precedent speaks to the objective justification for an initial warrantless arrest—not a continued restraint “pursuant to legal process,” where Manuel requires that the process maintaining custody be supported by probable cause. Justice Thomas’s causation concern is well-taken, yet it cuts against a categorical any-crime bar: the proper originalist/textualist limit is ordinary § 1983 causation—no Fourth Amendment injury absent proof the baseless charge caused incremental detention, higher bail, or materially harsher conditions. Thompson’s reliance on the malicious-prosecution analogue at the time of § 1983’s enactment reinforces that the “without probable cause” inquiry is naturally charge-specific as to the charge that produced the additional restraint, while causation and damages prevent transforming the claim into a free-floating overcharging tort. Treating one valid count as insulating knowingly unsupported added counts would sever the Fourth Amendment reasonableness inquiry from the legal process actually used to restrain liberty.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Justice Alito’s Devenpeck argument remains the strongest for Respondent, but I agree with Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kagan that Devenpeck’s any-offense principle is tethered to initial warrantless arrest justification and does not answer Manuel’s distinct inquiry into continued restraint “pursuant to legal process” that is allegedly unsupported by probable cause as to the charge that drove that process. Justice Thomas’s causation insistence is persuasive as a limiting principle: absent proof the baseless charge caused incremental detention, higher bail, or materially harsher conditions, there is no Fourth Amendment injury attributable to that charge—but that cuts against a categorical any-crime bar and instead supports a charge-specific claim with a real causation requirement. Thompson’s malicious-prosecution analogue, as Justice Barrett notes, makes it procedurally fair and practically sensible to focus on whether the particular charge used to justify added restraints lacked probable cause, while leaving damages and proximate cause to prevent overbroad liability. On a pragmatic view of real-world pretrial practice, an any-crime rule would too readily immunize unsupported add-on counts that foreseeably worsen restraint, which is inconsistent with the Fourth Amendment’s demand that legal process be grounded in probable cause for the restraints it produces.

John Roberts.reasoning: Under the Fourth Amendment as applied through § 1983, a plaintiff may state a claim for an unreasonable seizure pursuant to legal process when detention or other pretrial restraints are caused by charges lacking probable cause. Manuel v. City of Joliet held the Fourth Amendment continues to govern post-process pretrial detention, and Thompson v. Clark treated the claim’s most analogous tort as malicious prosecution—pointing to a charge-specific inquiry rooted in the presence or absence of probable cause and causation. A categorical “any-crime” rule risks insulating baseless charges that foreseeably add to the severity or duration of the seizure, which would be inconsistent with the Fourth Amendment’s probable-cause requirement; the ruling can be kept narrow by requiring proof that the unsupported charge caused incremental restraint or prolonged detention. This approach respects precedent and institutional limits by rejecting a broad immunity rule while leaving lower courts to apply ordinary causation and damages principles to determine whether the baseless charge made a material difference to the seizure.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment prohibits an "unreasonable" seizure, and where legal process results in a seizure independently supported by probable cause for at least one charge, the seizure is not unreasonable as a matter of constitutional text and original public meaning. Section 1983 provides a cause of action only for the deprivation of a federal right; importing the common-law malicious-prosecution element of "without probable cause" (Thompson v. Clark) should not convert a charge-by-charge defect into a Fourth Amendment violation when the seizure would have occurred anyway on a valid charge. Manuel v. City of Joliet recognizes Fourth Amendment scrutiny of pretrial detention pursuant to legal process, but it does not compel a charge-specific rule that disregards the overall reasonableness and causation of the seizure. Absent proof that the baseless count itself caused additional seizure (prolonged detention or materially harsher conditions), there is no Fourth Amendment injury attributable to that count.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment asks whether the seizure was reasonable, and under Devenpeck v. Alford probable cause for any offense known to the officers suffices to justify the seizure even if the stated charge is unsupported. Manuel v. City of Joliet and Thompson v. Clark confirm that malicious-prosecution-type § 1983 claims are anchored in the Fourth Amendment’s prohibition on unreasonable seizures pursuant to legal process, which points to evaluating the legality of the seizure as a whole rather than parsing each charge in the abstract. If a plaintiff was lawfully seized and held on at least one charge supported by probable cause, imposing Fourth Amendment liability for a simultaneous unsupported charge risks converting § 1983 into a broad charge-by-charge tort and would predictably chill legitimate law-enforcement charging decisions without a clear textual basis in the Amendment. Absent a concrete showing that the unsupported charge itself caused a distinct increase in the duration or severity of the seizure, the Fourth Amendment injury is not established.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s protection against unreasonable seizures applies not only to an initial arrest but also to post-legal-process pretrial restraint, and officers violate it when they cause a seizure “pursuant to legal process but without probable cause.” Manuel v. City of Joliet holds that unlawful pretrial detention based on fabricated or unsupported allegations states a Fourth Amendment claim, and Thompson v. Clark confirms § 1983 liability where a malicious-prosecution-type deprivation results in a seizure. A categorical “any-crime” rule would perversely insulate officers who add baseless charges that foreseeably increase bail, restrictions, or leverage—real, practical deprivations of liberty that the Fourth Amendment guards against—even if another charge had probable cause. The better rule is charge-specific: if the unsupported charge caused or prolonged a seizure (including conditions of release), a plaintiff may pursue a Fourth Amendment claim under § 1983, with causation and damages handled in the ordinary way.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment prohibits an unreasonable “seizure pursuant to legal process,” and Manuel v. City of Joliet makes clear that post-process pretrial detention remains governed by the Fourth Amendment when maintained without probable cause. A categorical any-crime rule is textually and practically overbroad because it treats the seizure as automatically reasonable even if officers initiate or sustain an additional charge lacking probable cause that foreseeably increases the duration or severity of the resulting restraints (detention, bail, conditions), undermining the Amendment’s probable-cause requirement. Consistent with Thompson v. Clark’s use of common-law malicious-prosecution principles while tailoring them to the Fourth Amendment, the better rule is charge-specific causation: the plaintiff must show the baseless charge caused or prolonged a Fourth Amendment seizure beyond what the supported charge would have produced. That approach preserves workability (by requiring proof of incremental restraint and causation) without immunizing fabrication or reckless overcharging simply because another charge had probable cause.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s text forbids “unreasonable seizures,” and a seizure “pursuant to legal process” is unreasonable to the extent it is grounded on a charge lacking probable cause and that charge caused or prolonged the restraint; probable cause for a different, simultaneous charge does not categorically erase the constitutional defect. Manuel v. City of Joliet confirms the Fourth Amendment governs post-process pretrial detention and leaves courts to supply the claim’s elements under § 1983, whose text requires a causal connection between the challenged conduct and the injury. Thompson v. Clark likewise recognizes a Fourth Amendment “malicious-prosecution” analogue under § 1983 focused on seizure pursuant to legal process, not a blanket any-crime immunity. Separation-of-powers principles counsel against judicially creating an atextual “any-crime” bar; instead, plaintiffs must prove lack of probable cause as to the challenged charge and causation as to the seizure’s duration or conditions.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Under the Fourth Amendment and § 1983, the proper focus is whether the plaintiff suffered an unreasonable seizure pursuant to legal process, and whether the specific challenged charge lacked probable cause and caused or prolonged that seizure. Manuel v. City of Joliet makes clear that the Fourth Amendment continues to govern post-legal-process pretrial detention, and it directs courts to define the claim’s contours by looking to the most analogous common-law tort and the Amendment’s values and purposes. Thompson v. Clark reinforces that approach by anchoring the analysis in 1871 malicious-prosecution principles, which were charge-specific and keyed to causation, not an “any-crime” categorical bar. A workable, precedent-consistent rule is that probable cause for one charge does not automatically defeat liability for another baseless charge if that charge foreseeably imposed additional restraints or extended detention, with causation and damages doing the limiting work.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment governs “seizures pursuant to legal process,” and under Manuel v. City of Joliet we look to the common-law malicious-prosecution analogue at the time § 1983 was enacted to define the claim’s contours, including the requirement that the challenged process be instituted “without probable cause.” Thompson v. Clark confirms that lack-of-probable-cause is an element of the Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution claim and, consistent with ordinary tort principles of causation and damages, that inquiry is best understood charge-specifically when a baseless count foreseeably causes or prolongs the seizure (e.g., higher bail or added restrictions) even if another count had probable cause. An “any-crime” rule would effectively immunize officers for initiating unsupported charges so long as one supported charge exists, a result difficult to reconcile with the Fourth Amendment’s text requiring reasonableness tied to the legal process actually used to restrain liberty. Precedent and methodological consistency thus favor permitting a claim when the plaintiff can show the unsupported charge caused additional Fourth Amendment harm notwithstanding simultaneous probable cause for another charge.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment protects against unreasonable seizures, including continued pretrial restraint pursuant to legal process, and § 1983 provides a remedy when officers cause such restraint without probable cause. Under Manuel v. City of Joliet, the Fourth Amendment “governs” unlawful pretrial detention beyond the start of legal process, and the relevant inquiry is whether the challenged legal process was supported by probable cause; a categorical “any-crime” rule would permit officers to add baseless counts with impunity even when those counts foreseeably increase bail, conditions, or detention. Thompson v. Clark confirms that this species of claim looks to common-law malicious prosecution principles, which focus on the absence of probable cause for the proceeding at issue, and nothing in Albright v. Oliver suggests the Fourth Amendment allows unsupported charges to escape scrutiny merely because another charge had probable cause. Procedural fairness and practical consequences counsel that courts should allow a charge-specific claim where the baseless charge caused or prolonged the seizure, with causation and damages handled through ordinary proof standards rather than a categorical bar.

case_analysis.focal_point: Whether a plaintiff can maintain a Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution claim under § 1983 for a baseless charge that contributed to a seizure when at least one other contemporaneous charge was supported by probable cause.
case_analysis.legal_provision: U.S. Const. amend. IV (Fourth Amendment); 42 U.S.C. § 1983
case_analysis.petitioner_position: Petitioners argue the Sixth Circuit’s “any-crime” or “any-valid-charge” rule wrongly bars Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution liability whenever probable cause exists for at least one charge, even if officers also initiated an unsupported charge that foreseeably caused or prolonged a criminal-process seizure. They contend Fourth Amendment reasonableness must be assessed charge-specifically (or at least allow liability where the baseless charge caused additional liberty restrictions), consistent with the Warrant Clause’s particularity requirement and the principle that fabricated or unsupported charges can independently inflict constitutional harm (e.g., added bail conditions, travel restrictions, court appearances, reputational and economic harms, or increased detention risk). Petitioners and supporting amici emphasize that an any-crime rule creates perverse incentives to stack extra charges without probable cause and dilutes accountability for initiating wrongful criminal process.
case_analysis.respondent_position: Respondents argue a Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution claim fails if the plaintiff’s seizure was justified by probable cause for any one of the charges brought, because the Constitution prohibits unreasonable seizures—not unreasonable charges in the abstract—and a seizure supported by probable cause is reasonable. They contend petitioners must, at minimum, prove that the unsupported charge changed the nature or duration of the seizure (e.g., caused longer detention or more onerous conditions) and that courts should not presume each charge independently alters the seizure. Respondents and supporting amici (including local-government and state amici) emphasize administrability and causation concerns, warning that allowing liability despite an independently supported charge would expand § 1983 exposure, invite speculative damages, and require courts to parse prosecutorial decisions and charging practices in ways that exceed the Fourth Amendment’s focus on seizure justification.

John Roberts.reasoning: Justice Kagan and Justice Barrett most forcefully argue from the Fourth Amendment’s particularity logic and the risk of charge-stacking, but under Manuel and Thompson the constitutional injury remains a seizure “resulting” from legal process that lacks probable cause—so liability must turn on whether the unsupported charge actually caused additional restraint in duration or conditions. Their approach is persuasive insofar as it rejects a categorical any-valid-charge safe harbor, yet it does not undermine my view that the Fourth Amendment does not constitutionalize wrong-charge allegations absent proof of an incremental seizure; causation does the narrowing work, consistent with institutional legitimacy concerns about turning §1983 into generalized oversight of charging. Justice Sotomayor’s emphasis on foreseeability reinforces the proximate-cause inquiry, but it still presupposes a demonstrable seizure increment rather than a label-based wrong. I therefore remain with respondents: a plaintiff must prove the baseless count was a but-for and proximate cause of materially worsened detention beyond what the supported charge would have produced.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s “charge-specific plus causation” framework is the strongest petitioner argument because it tries to keep the inquiry tethered to incremental restraint while avoiding an any-valid-charge safe harbor. But even with a causation element, their approach implicitly treats the absence of probable cause for a particular count as a Fourth Amendment defect in the legal process itself, rather than asking the textually grounded question Manuel and Thompson pose: whether the prosecution "resulted in" (i.e., caused) an unreasonable seizure in fact—added duration or materially harsher conditions beyond what a supported charge would have produced, as the Chief Justice and Justice Kavanaugh emphasize. The Warrant Clause’s particularity principle constrains what a warrant authorizes; it does not constitutionalize charge-label accuracy absent a demonstrable change in the seizure’s scope, and I would not expand § 1983 into generalized supervision of charging decisions. Thompson and Manuel therefore reinforce—not undermine—a causation-to-added-restraint limitation that defeats liability where the seizure would have been identical on a valid charge.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: Justice Barrett and Justice Kagan persuasively invoke the Fourth Amendment’s particularity logic and the practical risk of charge-stacking, but under a textual focus on “seizures,” that concern cannot itself create liability absent proof the unsupported count actually produced additional restraint. Chief Justice Roberts’s causation limitation best fits Manuel’s framing of the injury as detention unsupported by probable cause and Thompson v. Clark’s requirement that the prosecution “resulted in a seizure,” which in practical terms demands but-for and proximate causation of added duration or conditions beyond what the valid charge would have imposed. I therefore reject an absolute any-valid-charge safe harbor only to the extent it blocks plaintiffs from proving incremental seizure harm, but I cannot accept petitioners’ charge-by-charge theory that would constitutionalize charging labels untethered to a materially worsened seizure. Justice Thomas is right that the Fourth Amendment does not supply a freestanding wrong-charge inquiry, and the administrable constitutional line is added-restraint causation, not abstract charge accuracy.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s insistence that the Fourth Amendment injury must be a seizure—and that the baseless charge must be a but-for and proximate cause of added duration or harsher conditions—is the right limiting principle, and I accept it as an element of the claim. But Justice Thomas’s further move from that premise to practical immunity whenever any charge is supported goes too far: Manuel and Thompson focus on detention “pursuant to legal process” that “resulted in a seizure,” which is satisfied when an unsupported count foreseeably helps authorize, extend, or intensify custody beyond what the supported count would have produced. On my pragmatic view, an any-valid-charge safe harbor would predictably reward charge-stacking and shift the costs onto indigent and overpoliced defendants, while a causation-limited, charge-specific rule preserves administrability and keeps damages tethered to incremental restraint rather than mere mislabeling. Because respondents’ best arguments refine—rather than undermine—this causation-centered approach, I do not change my vote.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s causation-to-added-restraint point is the strongest respondent argument, and I agree it properly cabins the claim: the Fourth Amendment injury is the seizure, so the plaintiff must prove the unsupported charge was a but-for and proximate cause of additional duration or conditions. But that same premise defeats an any-valid-charge categorical bar, because under Manuel the question is whether legal process lacking probable cause foreseeably contributed to authorizing or maintaining the detention, not whether some other charge could have justified custody in the abstract. Justice Thomas’s Albright/Wallace concern does not undermine this: those cases relocate the right to the Fourth Amendment rather than creating immunity for baseless legal-process grounds that actually affect the seizure. Thompson’s “resulted in a seizure” language fits naturally with a causation element and does not require collapsing the inquiry into a one-valid-charge solvent, so I remain with a charge-specific probable-cause inquiry plus a real causation requirement.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Chief Justice’s and Justice Kavanaugh’s causation-to-added-restraint requirement is the strongest respondent point, but it cuts against any categorical any-valid-charge bar: once the plaintiff plausibly alleges the unsupported charge was a but-for and proximate cause of additional custody or conditions, the seizure is unreasonable to that extent under Manuel’s Fourth Amendment framing. Justice Thomas’s invocation of Albright and Wallace does not supply an immunity rule; those cases reject substantive due process and redirect the inquiry to the Fourth Amendment, where the Warrant Clause’s particularity logic (as Justice Barrett notes) resists treating probable cause for one offense as an all-purpose solvent for other baseless legal process that foreseeably alters the seizure. Thompson’s “resulted in a seizure” language fits comfortably with making incremental restraint causation an element, not with foreclosing suit whenever any charge is supported. The administrable, text-rooted rule is therefore charge-specific probable-cause scrutiny coupled with a real, damages-limiting causation requirement—not a safe harbor for charge-stacking.

Brett Kavanaugh.reasoning: Justice Barrett’s and Justice Kagan’s particularity/charge-stacking concern powerfully shows why there should be no categorical any-valid-charge “safe harbor,” and I agree with them—and with Justice Sotomayor—that causation must do the limiting work. But as Chief Justice Roberts emphasizes from Manuel and Thompson, the Fourth Amendment injury is a seizure that is unreasonable in its fact, scope, or duration, and Thompson’s requirement that the prosecution “resulted in a seizure” means the plaintiff must prove the baseless charge was a but-for and proximate cause of added restraint beyond what the supported charge would have produced. The opposing side’s charge-specific framing risks sliding into liability based on charge labels alone (or presumed incremental harm) rather than a demonstrated incremental seizure, which would untether the tort from the Amendment’s text and practical administration. I therefore stay with respondents: allow claims only where the unsupported charge actually prolonged or aggravated the seizure or its conditions.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts’s causation-to-added-restraint limitation is the strongest respondent point, and I agree the Fourth Amendment claim must be tethered to a seizure injury that the unsupported charge but-for and proximately caused—no damages for a “wrong label” alone. But that causation requirement undercuts, rather than supports, an any-valid-charge safe harbor at the liability stage: the Fourth Amendment’s original public meaning and its particularity logic do not treat probable cause for one offense as a universal solvent for other legal-process grounds that foreseeably authorize or maintain custody. Justice Thomas’s reliance on Albright and Wallace does not move me because those cases reject substantive due process and relocate the inquiry to the Fourth Amendment; they do not adopt a categorical any-charge rule, and Manuel and Thompson instead focus on whether the challenged legal process resulted in an unreasonable seizure—which is satisfied when the baseless charge actually adds restraint. Administrability concerns Justice Kavanaugh raises are answered by making incremental-seizure causation an element of the claim, rather than immunizing charge-stacking whenever the State can point to any valid count.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: Chief Justice Roberts and Justice Kavanaugh press the strongest respondent point: the Fourth Amendment injury is the seizure, so liability must be tied to a baseless charge only if it but-for and proximately caused additional restraint beyond what a supported charge would have produced. I agree with that limiting principle, but it cuts against—rather than supports—any categorical any-valid-charge bar, because Manuel’s “pursuant to legal process” framework and Thompson’s requirement that the prosecution “resulted in a seizure” naturally accommodate a charge-specific inquiry with a real causation element. Justice Thomas’s Albright/Wallace concern about constitutionalizing charging decisions is answered by making incremental seizure harm an essential element, which both cabins damages and preserves administrability while avoiding an incentive for charge-stacking (as Justice Sotomayor notes) that would predictably burden defendants least able to contest it. On my pragmatic, procedure-centered approach, the rule should vindicate Fourth Amendment fairness without turning every overcharge into a standalone constitutional tort.

John Roberts.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment addresses unreasonable seizures, and where a plaintiff’s contemporaneous seizure is supported by probable cause for at least one charge, the seizure is presumptively reasonable unless the plaintiff can show the baseless charge itself caused additional restraint or prolonged detention. Manuel v. City of Joliet makes clear that the Fourth Amendment governs not only the initiation but also the duration of pretrial detention, so liability should turn on whether the unsupported charge extended the seizure beyond what the valid charge justified, not on a freestanding defect in charging. A narrow causation-based rule preserves § 1983’s remedial function without collapsing into a charge-by-charge presumption that risks overdeterrence and speculative damages, and it aligns with Thompson v. Clark’s insistence that we identify the specific Fourth Amendment injury at issue.

Clarence Thomas.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment speaks to the “reasonableness” of a “seizure,” not to the validity of each charging label attached to it; where probable cause exists for at least one contemporaneous offense supporting the seizure, the seizure is constitutionally reasonable, and § 1983 supplies no freestanding remedy for an “unreasonable charge.” See U.S. Const. amend. IV; 42 U.S.C. § 1983; Albright v. Oliver (1994) (rejecting substantive-due-process malicious-prosecution theory and directing plaintiffs to the Fourth Amendment’s text). Manuel v. City of Joliet (2017) confirms Fourth Amendment scrutiny turns on whether custody is supported by probable cause, not on the correctness of every prosecutorial theory, and Wallace v. Kato (2007) similarly frames the injury around detention without probable cause. Absent proof that the unsupported charge itself caused additional restraint beyond the seizure justified by the supported charge, petitioners’ theory would expand the Fourth Amendment beyond its original public meaning and invite speculative, charge-by-charge damages untethered to the seizure’s legality.

Samuel Alito.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment bars unreasonable seizures, not the mere addition of an allegedly unsupported charge, and a seizure supported by probable cause is ordinarily reasonable. Manuel v. City of Joliet instructs courts to identify the specific constitutional right at issue, but it does not compel a charge-by-charge regime that would impose § 1983 liability where the plaintiff would have been seized anyway on a valid charge; the proper inquiry is whether the baseless charge actually caused a material change in the nature or duration of the seizure. Adopting petitioners’ charge-specific rule would expand § 1983 exposure and invite speculative causation and damages assessments untethered to the seizure’s justification, contrary to the Fourth Amendment’s focus and § 1983’s remedial limits. Thompson v. Clark recognized a Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution-type claim, but it did not displace the requirement that the plaintiff show an unreasonable seizure attributable to the challenged conduct rather than a seizure independently justified by probable cause.

Sonia Sotomayor.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment requires that seizures be reasonable and grounded in probable cause tied to the justification offered, and under Manuel v. City of Joliet (2017) courts must “identify the specific constitutional right” at issue when assessing a § 1983 claim—here, an unreasonable seizure pursuant to legal process based on an unsupported charge. An “any-valid-charge” rule would improperly immunize officers who initiate baseless accusations that foreseeably cause or prolong liberty restraints, undermining § 1983’s remedial purpose and the Fourth Amendment’s particularized protections. Thompson v. Clark (2022) confirms that Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution claims target wrongful criminal-process seizures, and where an unsupported charge contributes to the seizure’s imposition or continuation, liability should turn on that charge’s causal role rather than the mere existence of probable cause for some other charge. Administrability and damages concerns can be handled through ordinary causation limits (and Heck v. Humphrey (1994) where applicable), not by a categorical bar that invites charge-stacking against vulnerable people.

Elena Kagan.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s text and structure focus on the reasonableness of a particular seizure as justified by specific factual showings of probable cause, and its Warrant Clause particularity requirement cuts against an “any-valid-charge” approach that immunizes knowingly or recklessly baseless accusations. Manuel v. City of Joliet instructs that in § 1983 suits courts must “identify the specific constitutional right” at issue and recognizes Fourth Amendment scrutiny of post-legal-process detention when it is “unsupported by probable cause,” which fits a charge-specific inquiry where an unsupported charge foreseeably causes or prolongs the seizure. At the same time, consistent with workability and causation limits, liability should require proof that the baseless charge actually contributed to additional detention or more onerous conditions beyond what the supported charge would have produced, rather than presuming incremental restraint. Thompson v. Clark’s Fourth Amendment grounding for malicious-prosecution-type claims reinforces that the constitutional harm is seizure through legal process without probable cause, not merely the presence of some valid charge in the mix.

Neil Gorsuch.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s text forbids “unreasonable seizures,” and a seizure becomes unreasonable when it is caused or prolonged by the government’s initiation of criminal process on a charge lacking probable cause, even if another contemporaneous charge was supported. Section 1983 supplies a remedy for the violation of that specific constitutional right, and our cases instruct courts to identify the particular right at issue and test the detention’s justification against probable cause. See Manuel v. City of Joliet, 580 U.S. 357, 370 (2017). A categorical any-valid-charge rule improperly treats probable cause as an all-purpose talisman, ignoring the Warrant Clause’s charge-particularity logic and allowing baseless accusations to escape accountability when they foreseeably impose additional restraints; causation and damages can be addressed by requiring the plaintiff to show the unsupported charge contributed to the seizure’s nature or duration. Thompson v. Clark (2022) confirms the Fourth Amendment framework for these claims and does not require importing a blanket any-crime bar.

Thompson v. Clark expressly notes that a Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution plaintiff “has to prove that the malicious prosecution resulted in a seizure,” and Manuel v. City of Joliet likewise ties Fourth Amendment liability to detention/seizure without probable cause, making causation to the seizure an element rather than a damages-only inquiry. Where contemporaneous probable cause independently justified the seizure, liability for an additional baseless charge should require proof that the unsupported charge caused a distinct increase in the nature or duration of the seizure; that approach is more workable and avoids expanding § 1983 beyond its text as a remedy for constitutional (seizure) violations. In my view, the Sixth Circuit’s any-valid-charge rule may be overbroad in some applications, but the Constitution’s focus on the reasonableness of the seizure supports respondents’ causation-limiting principle here.

Amy Coney Barrett.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s text protects against unreasonable “seizures,” and under Manuel v. City of Joliet, 580 U.S. 357 (2017), the threshold inquiry in a § 1983 suit is to identify the specific constitutional right at issue—here, whether the challenged criminal-process seizure was reasonable as to the asserted basis for that seizure. An “any-valid-charge” rule is difficult to square with the Amendment’s warrant particularity logic and risks insulating officers from liability for initiating a baseless charge that foreseeably caused or prolonged a seizure, even when another charge had probable cause. Thompson v. Clark, 596 U.S. 36 (2022), confirms that a Fourth Amendment malicious-prosecution-type claim is cognizable under § 1983 and looks to common-law analogues, which historically allowed recovery when some charges were unsupported notwithstanding others being supported, so long as the unsupported charge caused a seizure-related deprivation. Respondents’ causation concerns are properly handled as an element of the claim—requiring proof that the baseless charge contributed to the nature or duration of the seizure—rather than by an absolute bar whenever any probable cause exists.

Ketanji Brown Jackson.reasoning: The Fourth Amendment’s protection against “unreasonable seizures” and § 1983’s remedial purpose are ill-served by an “any-valid-charge” rule that immunizes officers who initiate baseless charges that foreseeably cause or prolong criminal-process restraints, even if some contemporaneous charge had probable cause. Manuel v. City of Joliet instructs courts to “identify the specific constitutional right” at issue and recognizes that post-process detention without probable cause is a Fourth Amendment harm, which supports evaluating probable cause and causation in a charge-specific way when an unsupported charge materially contributes to the seizure’s initiation, duration, or conditions. Thompson v. Clark likewise ties the claim to whether the malicious prosecution “resulted in a seizure,” allowing liability where the baseless charge is a but-for and proximate cause of added liberty restrictions. Practically and procedurally, rejecting the any-crime rule reduces incentives to stack unsupported charges and better vindicates equal protection and fairness in the criminal process while still requiring plaintiffs to prove causation and damages.
